## order-debounce.ts (core)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern debounce
 * @options c3072a2218bc8955
 */

/**
 * Where the delay comes from.
 *
 * A port rather than a direct call to `setTimeout`, which is what lets a test
 * drive the clock instead of waiting on it. The alternative is the framework's
 * fake timers, and those are a different API in each one — a poor dependency
 * for a file that is also expected to run under a hand-written assertion shim.
 *
 * It hands back a function that stops the timer, rather than a handle to pass
 * to a clearing function. That is deliberate: the handle is a `number` in a
 * browser and an object in Node, so a type naming it is wrong in one of the
 * two, and every implementation of this port already knows how to cancel its
 * own.
 */
export interface OrderDebounceTimers {
  readonly delay: (ms: number, callback: () => void) => () => void;
}

/**
 * The port over whatever timers the runtime provides.
 *
 * The default, so that ordinary use needs no argument and only a test has to
 * supply one.
 */
export const orderSystemTimers: OrderDebounceTimers = {
  delay: (ms, callback) => {
    const handle = setTimeout(callback, ms);
    return () => {
      clearTimeout(handle);
    };
  },
};

/**
 * How long to wait, and what to wait with.
 *
 * `maxWaitMs` is the ceiling on the delay, and it is what keeps a caller who
 * never goes quiet from never being served. It is validated against `waitMs`
 * rather than merely documented, because a ceiling below the wait can never
 * take effect and is therefore always a mistake.
 *
 * `onError` is required, not optional. Nothing here returns the failure to a
 * caller, so this is the only place one can go — and a discarded rejection ends
 * a Node process rather than being ignored.
 */
export interface OrderDebounceOptions {
  readonly waitMs: number;
  /** The longest a call may be held, however many arrive. */
  readonly maxWaitMs: number;
  readonly onError: (error: unknown) => void;
  /** Defaults to the runtime's own timers. */
  readonly timers?: OrderDebounceTimers;
}

/**
 * The debounced function, and the three things worth being able to do to it.
 *
 * `cancel` is what an interface element needs when it goes away with a call
 * outstanding; `flush` is what one needs when it goes away and the call should
 * still happen — a draft saved on close. Both are the difference between a
 * debounce that is usable in a component lifecycle and one that is not.
 *
 * `pending` reports whether a call is waiting. Worth having for the same
 * reason: "is there unsaved work" is a question the caller cannot otherwise
 * answer.
 *
 * The result type is a parameter only where there is a result. The void
 * rendering returns nothing, so a second parameter would appear in the type's
 * name and nowhere in its body — which a project compiling with
 * `noUnusedLocals` reports, and which is misleading whether or not they do.
 */
export interface OrderDebounced<A extends readonly unknown[]> {
  (...args: A): void;
  /** Drops the pending call. */
  readonly cancel: () => void;
  /** Runs the pending call now, if there is one. */
  readonly flush: () => void;
  readonly pending: () => boolean;
}

/**
 * Wraps a function so that a burst of calls becomes one call.
 *
 * Invoked on the first call of a burst and again at the end if any others
 * arrived. A single call invokes exactly once — the trailing invocation is
 * skipped when nothing was suppressed, which is the defect that separates a
 * correct implementation of this edge from the obvious one.
 *
 * Nothing is returned. A caller who needs the result wants the promise
 * rendering of this pattern; this one is for a handler whose only job is the
 * side effect.
 */
export function debounceOrder<A extends readonly unknown[], R>(
  fn: (...args: A) => Promise<R> | R,
  options: OrderDebounceOptions,
): OrderDebounced<A> {
  const { waitMs, maxWaitMs } = options;
  const timers = options.timers ?? orderSystemTimers;

  if (!Number.isFinite(waitMs) || waitMs < 0) {
    throw new RangeError(
      `waitMs must be a non-negative finite number, received ${String(waitMs)}`,
    );
  }

  // Refused rather than documented. A ceiling below the wait can never take
  // effect, so it is always a mistake, and one whose only symptom is an option
  // that appears to do nothing.
  if (!Number.isFinite(maxWaitMs) || maxWaitMs < waitMs) {
    throw new RangeError(
      `maxWaitMs ${String(maxWaitMs)} must be a finite number at least as large as waitMs ${String(waitMs)}`,
    );
  }

  // `active` is the burst, not the pending call, and the difference is
  // load-bearing: a ceiling invocation empties the pending call while the burst
  // continues, and treating the next call as a fresh leading edge would then
  // invoke twice in a row.
  let active = false;
  /** Calls received since the last invocation. Not since the burst began. */
  let pendingCalls = 0;
  let latest: A | undefined = undefined;
  let stopQuiet: (() => void) | undefined = undefined;
  let stopCeiling: (() => void) | undefined = undefined;

  const invoke = (args: A): Promise<R> => {
    pendingCalls = 0;

    // Started here, synchronously, before anything is awaited. Two
    // consequences, both wanted: a call made from inside `fn` belongs to the
    // next burst rather than this one, and a failure is attached to below
    // rather than escaping.
    const outcome = (async () => await fn(...args))();

    // Reported rather than dropped. Without a caller to reject there is nowhere
    // else for it to go, and an unhandled rejection is fatal to a Node process
    // rather than merely untidy.
    outcome.catch((error: unknown) => {
      options.onError(error);
    });

    return outcome;
  };

  const endBurst = (): void => {
    active = false;
    stopQuiet = undefined;
    stopCeiling?.();
    stopCeiling = undefined;
  };

  const onQuiet = (): void => {
    const args = latest;

    // `pendingCalls` is what stops a single call invoking twice under this
    // edge: the leading invocation cleared it, so a burst of one arrives here
    // with nothing suppressed to run.
    const due = pendingCalls > 0 && args !== undefined;

    endBurst();

    if (due) void invoke(args);
  };

  const onCeiling = (): void => {
    stopCeiling = undefined;
    const args = latest;

    if (pendingCalls === 0 || args === undefined) return;

    void invoke(args);

    // The burst is not over, so the quiet timer is left alone and a fresh
    // ceiling is started from *this* expiry rather than from the next call.
    // Armed from the next call instead, the interval drifts by the gap between
    // calls and the guarantee quietly weakens.
    stopCeiling = timers.delay(maxWaitMs, onCeiling);
  };

  const debounced = (...args: A): void => {
    latest = args;
    pendingCalls += 1;
    const leadingEdge = !active;
    active = true;

    stopQuiet?.();
    stopQuiet = timers.delay(waitMs, onQuiet);

    // Not restarted if one is already running, and that guard is the point of
    // the option. Reset alongside the quiet timer, neither would ever expire
    // under continuous calls and the ceiling would silently do nothing at all.
    if (stopCeiling === undefined) {
      stopCeiling = timers.delay(maxWaitMs, onCeiling);
    }

    if (leadingEdge) {
      void invoke(args);
      return;
    }
  };

  return Object.assign(debounced, {
    cancel: (): void => {
      pendingCalls = 0;
      latest = undefined;
      stopQuiet?.();
      endBurst();
    },

    flush: (): void => {
      if (stopQuiet === undefined) return;

      // Cancelled before it is run by hand. `onQuiet` cannot do it — it is
      // normally reached *by* that timer — so a flush that skipped this leaves
      // a timer scheduled, which in Node holds the process open long after the
      // work is done.
      stopQuiet();
      onQuiet();
    },

    pending: (): boolean => pendingCalls > 0,
  });
}
```

## order-debounce-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern debounce
 * @options c3072a2218bc8955
 */

/**
 * Search as the user types.
 *
 * The case that names the pattern: a keystroke is not a request, and issuing
 * one per keystroke spends a request on every prefix of what the user meant to
 * type.
 */

import { debounceOrder } from "./order-debounce.js";
import type { OrderDebounced } from "./order-debounce.js";

/**
 * Searches once the typing settles, and shows what came back.
 *
 * The ceiling matters more here than it appears to. Someone typing steadily for
 * ten seconds never pauses for the full wait, and without it they would see
 * nothing at all until they stopped.
 *
 * Nothing is returned, so the failure handler given at construction is the only
 * place an error can go. A caller needing to await the search wants the promise
 * rendering instead.
 *
 * `cancel` and `flush` are forwarded rather than hidden, because the component
 * holding this is the thing that knows when it is going away.
 */
export function searchAsYouType(
  search: (term: string) => Promise<readonly string[]>,
  show: (results: readonly string[]) => void,
): OrderDebounced<[string]> {
  return debounceOrder(
    async (term: string) => {
      show(await search(term));
    },
    {
      waitMs: 300,
      maxWaitMs: 2_000,
      onError: (error: unknown) => {
        console.error("search failed", error);
      },
    },
  );
}
```
